source.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a complete post and comment thread, but the post is a linkpost summary rather than the full linked paper.
record.tranche_reason: It reports comparisons in which sparse-autoencoder features are more interpretable than individual neurons, including an automated description-scoring result. This challenges or refines neuron-level interpretability, but does not reproduce the Qwen3 pole audit.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative human and automated comparisons of neurons with learned features. It does not report a proportion of neurons with one or two jobs, or results for the claim's Qwen3 pole categories. A commenter quotes rubric medians from the paper; those are noted in a row but are not treated as independent new experiments.
record.test_reason: The study's own human rating of a small one-layer transformer's MLP neurons is a median neuron score of 0, meaning no hypothesis could be formed. This bears against V2, the claim that most neurons in other language models have one main job. The autointerp comparison shows only that neurons score below features. With no absolute scores, it cannot show V7's minority share.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that individual neurons are largely uninterpretable or polysemantic, a roadblock that features overcome. They present features as the better unit, and say scaling to frontier models is now mainly an engineering problem.
record.recipe_differences: The post summarizes sparse-autoencoder feature decomposition and compares neurons with learned features; it does not use the Qwen3 neuron-pole audit method or measure the essay's pole categories.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse-autoencoder features score higher than neurons on both human rubric ratings (median 12 vs 0) and automated activation prediction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned dictionary features are more interpretable than individual neurons in a small transformer.

record.problems: The post provides no absolute automated scores or fraction of neuron explanations judged good, and does not state that activation prediction was assessed on held-out new text. The supplied document is a summary rather than the full paper.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported results were omitted. The post's general mention of feature steering and feature universality does not give a result measuring any of the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or pole shares.
No mixture-of-experts, large or trillion-parameter models; no per-pole split; only one small one-layer model.
The cat-and-car neuron is cited as polysemantic, but whether it detects pose is not tested.
No variation of architecture, regularization or neuron-level tools; no vision estimates.
No attribution graphs or circuit analysis on neurons.
No comparison of explanations from activating examples against held-out firing.
No absolute simulation scores for neurons and no comparison of explainer strength, in the supplied text.

missing.what: Absolute automated-interpretability (simulation) score distributions for neurons, needed to test V7's minority share
missing.locator: Full paper, automated interpretability section (not in the supplied linkpost)

missing.what: Full distribution of human rubric scores for neurons (share above the 'interpretable' threshold of 8)
missing.locator: Full paper, human interpretability section; partly quoted in Raemon's comment

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text is a linkpost summary; the key neuron median comes from a comment quoting the paper. The study is not an original source. Neuron-level ratings here are whole-neuron and done without the essay's pole method or tools, which the essay (V4) would cite as the reason. So the V2 challenge applies to this setting and method only.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit, neuron-pole counts, or proportions of poles assigned one job, two related jobs, or not understood.
No cross-model or scale comparison of the stated shares; the small model's neuron-versus-feature interpretability comparison does not quantify those shares.
The cat-and-car example is mentioned, but the post does not test whether it detects pose or establish recursive generalization.
No test of architecture, regularization, tool quality, or the stated InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
No attribution-graph reconstruction or test of whether neurons suffice as circuit units.
No test of explanations based on activating examples against separately held-out firing examples.

The post reports that automated description-based activation prediction scores features higher than neurons, but gives no absolute rate of neurons scoring well, stronger-explainer comparison, or explicit held-out-new-text condition.

The study's own rubric gives a median neuron score of 0, so at least half of neurons had no hypothesis, versus V2's roughly 90% with one main job. The baseline field wrongly holds the feature score; the right reference is V2's share. The number comes from a comment quoting the paper, not the post body. Caveats: the rating is whole-neuron, not per pole, uses a rubric, and covers a one-layer model.
